title: The patient farmer (James 5:7–12)
hook: the farmer waits for the early and late rain

segments.voice: Yesterday, wages held back, and your line was the wages cry out. Which bill or debt did you pay sooner than you had to? Day six hundred seventy-nine.

You can't make a seed grow faster by yelling at it. Anyone who has kept a garden knows this. You plant. You water. Then you wait, and the waiting is most of the work. The Bible speaks of two rains in that land, the early rain and the latter rain. Commentators place the early one in autumn, softening hard ground for plowing and sowing, and the latter in spring, swelling the grain before harvest. Between them, months of watching the sky. James has just thundered at the rich who cheated their workers. Now he turns to his brethren, people waiting for things to be put right, and gives them a farmer to look at.

In the King James Bible: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." Husbandman is the old word for farmer. And the patience he has isn't passive. A farmer's waiting isn't idle. Farmers weed and mend fences and fix the plow. But they can't make it rain. They work hard on what they can do, and they wait for what they can't. Be patient like that, James says, and steady your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near. Then a practical warning for people under strain: "Grudge not one against another." When people wait a long time, they turn on each other. Look, the judge is standing at the door. Then James offers two more pictures of endurance. The prophets, who spoke for God and suffered for it. And then: "Ye have heard of the patience of Job." Patient as Job, people say. Yet in the book of Job, he doesn't sit quietly. He argues, he laments, he demands an answer from God. The Greek word James uses here means endurance, staying under the weight, and that is exactly what Job did. He complained loudly, and he didn't let go. And James says, you've seen how it ended: the Lord is full of pity and mercy. Last, a quick word about honesty: don't swear oaths. "Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." When you're waiting on God, keep your word plain. This week has been one long walk through James: faith and works, the tongue, wisdom from above, draw near, if the Lord wills, wages held back, and now the patient farmer.
screen: `JOB: LOUD, BUT HE DIDN'T LET GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're waiting on right now. A test result, a reply, a change in someone you love, a door that hasn't opened. Name it. Then sort it in two piles, like a farmer. What part of this can I work on? And what part is rain, out of my hands? Picture setting the rain part down. Then breathe into the waiting itself, without trying to hurry it. Notice if you feel any grudge rising toward someone in the waiting. If you pray, you can ask for patience. The bell holds the time.
Job. The example James gives of patience that still argues and laments loudly, enduring under the weight without letting go of God.
Your line: be patient. Today, when you catch yourself refreshing, checking or pushing on the thing you're waiting for, do one useful thing within your reach instead. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: James 5:7–10 is an Advent reading in some church lectionaries, in the season of waiting before Christmas, and Christians often turn to it in long illnesses or hard seasons.

original.note: Greek: endurance, literally remaining under. the word James uses for the patience of Job.

trapdoor: what you thought: wait quietly and don't complain.
what it means: work at what you can, wait for what you can't, don't turn on each other, and endure.
what a scholar hears: two Greek words, makrothymia (long-tempered) for the farmer and hypomonē (endurance) for Job; and Job's patience was anything but quiet.

notes: Early (autumn) and latter (spring) rains in the land of Israel: standard background (cf. Deuteronomy 11:14). Confirm.
James 5:7 uses μακροθυμέω for the farmer; 5:11 uses ὑπομονή for Job. Confirm.
The proverb 'the patience of Job' is commonly traced to James 5:11 in English Bibles. Confirm.
Week look-back covers days 673–679. Confirm the week boundary.
Use of James 5:7–10 in Advent (e.g. Third Sunday of Advent, Year A in the Revised Common Lectionary and Roman Lectionary): confirm.

Editor review (y2 669–687 pass): the autumn/spring rain seasons are now attributed to commentators (the cited texts name only early and latter rain); cut 'some of the busiest people on earth' and the unsourced claim that 'the patience of Job' became an English proverb (myth now says only that the phrase is in James); no longer tells the listener what they know about Job; 'the workers themselves' became 'his brethren', as 5:7 says; howItsDone softened.
